briefs.label: Morning Brief
briefs.title: Rescheduling Gains Ground Nationally, Michigan Operators Get Two Shots at Tax Relief
briefs.top: DEA's final Schedule III brief and a second straight Phase 3 win for Compass Pathways' psilocybin show real forward motion at the federal level, while Michigan operators now have two live paths out of the 24% wholesale tax squeeze — a September trial date and a GOP nominee vowing to roll it back. New storefronts opening and record 2025 sales volume prove demand for legal cannabis in Michigan is still rock-solid.

local.text: Michigan GOP gubernatorial nominee John James pledged in his new "Freedom Agenda" to repeal or significantly roll back the 24% wholesale cannabis tax, arguing it <cite index="62-1">"drives up prices, gives illegal operators a competitive edge, and has already fallen far short of revenue projections."</cite> He's also vowing to redirect enforcement toward illegal grow operations rather than licensed businesses, giving legal operators a clearer political path to relief heading into November.

The Michigan Cannabis Industry Association's original lawsuit against the 24% wholesale tax is <cite index="9-1">heading to trial in September</cite>, giving operators a real shot at rolling back the levy that's squeezed margins since January. A second suit argues the stacked tax creates unconstitutional "tax pyramiding" on top of the existing 10% excise and 6% sales taxes.

Common Citizen is set to open a new Eastpointe dispensary after <cite index="52-2">reaching a court-approved deal that gives it until Dec. 1 to fix up its building and start selling weed</cite>, adding a second legal retail option to a city currently served by just one shop.

Ann Arbor's The Jungle House just threw its grand-opening weekend, with early customers raving about <cite index="18-12">"a bunch of fire flower, really good prices, the vibes inside are awesome and totally different from every other place in town."</cite> Fresh storefronts still pulling crowds is proof there's real appetite for a strong retail experience, even in a saturated market.

Even with the tax squeeze on revenue, underlying demand is strong: <cite index="5-6,5-7">Michigan cannabis retailers sold more products in 2025 than in any year since the launch of adult-use sales</cite>. That volume growth is the foundation operators can build on once the wholesale tax fight resolves.

national.text: The DEA has filed its final brief formally urging the administrative law judge to move marijuana to Schedule III, <cite index="31-1">arguing that the evidence presented during the nearly three-week hearing shows the drug no longer meets the requirements for the nation's most restrictive drug category</cite>. A shift to Schedule III would <cite index="28-3">open up new banking opportunities and tax benefits for industry operators</cite> nationwide.

Congress kept the banking-reform push alive too — the bipartisan <cite index="31-7">SAFE Banking Act gains two new bipartisan cosponsors in the U.S. House</cite> in late August, adding momentum to efforts to give cannabis operators normal access to financial services.

Compass Pathways landed its second straight positive Phase 3 result for COMP360 psilocybin in treatment-resistant depression, posting <cite index="39-3">a highly statistically significant reduction in symptom severity (P<0.001) and a clinically meaningful difference of -3.8 points in change at the primary endpoint</cite>. The company says it's now <cite index="39-1">advancing our discussions with the FDA, with the goal of submitting an NDA in Q4 and securing approval</cite> — a potential first-ever approval for a classic psychedelic.

Curaleaf's hostile $272 million bid for Aurora Cannabis keeps escalating, with Aurora firing back that its own strategy is working — <cite index="42-4">net revenue is up 17% year-over-year, with the company's E.U. business thriving</cite> — while Curaleaf pushes shareholders directly to tender. Real consolidation cash is flowing into the sector even as the fight plays out.

Aurora isn't just playing defense — it recently closed its acquisition of Safari Flower to strengthen its medical cannabis position, and leadership is touting <cite index="45-1">its European manufacturing footprint, a key asset as North American cannabis firms jockey for a share of what most observers say is a steadily growing overseas market</cite>.
